Project Gallery

Submit your project

Share what you built with the class. The course team reviews each submission before it appears in the gallery.

This is a public submission. Approved projects appear in the Project Gallery, where anyone in the MIT community can see them. If you add a link, other people can open your project to test or use it, and you can ask them for feedback. Only share what you’re comfortable making visible.
Presented in class? If you submitted a PRD during the course, pick your project and we’ll fill in the details for you. If it’s an extra project with no PRD, skip this and fill in the form yourself.

Who built it? *
Try it (optional) Add a link only if you want other people to use or test your project.
Before you share a link, protect your costs and data. Anyone who has the link can use your project, and every use can spend your tokens, API requests or free-tier quota. So:
  • Set spending caps or usage limits on every paid tool and API key you use.
  • Keep API keys out of your code and public repositories; store them as environment variables.
  • Add a request limit or a sign-in so one person can’t use up your quota.
  • Don’t expose personal or sensitive data.
  • Start with a small group of testers. You can take the link down at any time.
Product Requirements Document (PRD) Optional. Attach it or link to it.

    File uploads aren’t available right now. Paste links to your PRD and screenshots instead.

    Builder toolkit

    Skills

    Share a skill you built, or download one from the class and use it in Claude.

    What is a skill?

    A skill is a small folder with a file called SKILL.md: a set of instructions (and, if you need them, extra files) that teaches Claude how to do one kind of task your way, such as reviewing a PRD or writing a weekly update. Claude loads it only when a task matches, so you don’t have to repeat yourself every time.

    You’re invited: share a skill with the class or download one from the list. The course team reviews shared skills first, but read any skill before you use it.

    Download a skill

    To use one: download the .zip, then upload it in Claude’s Skills settings (the menu name can vary).

    Idea Kick Starter

    Not sure where to start? Describe your idea in plain words and take a first step: three ways to start, a plan you can adjust, and a PDF to take to Claude.

    BetaThis tool is still in development, and some suggestions may contain errors. Treat them as ideas to explore, not as a final definition of how to build your project. Please don’t type personal or sensitive information.
    1. Your idea
    2. Choose a path
    3. Shape it
    4. Your plan

    Your idea

    Describe it in plain words: who it’s for and what problem it solves. A few sentences are enough.

    Choose a path

    Here are three ways to start the same idea, from lightest to most ambitious. Compare them, pick the one that fits you best, then press Next. Use “More details” if you want to know more about one.

    Your path in full

    Here is the full picture of the path you chose. Change or add anything you like, and tell us how much time you have.

    How much time do you have?

    Your plan

    Next: start your build in Claude. Upload this PDF to Claude to get your project going:
    1. Download the PDF.
    2. In Claude, create a new Project (Projects > New Project) and name it after your project.
    3. Upload the PDF to that Project.
    4. Paste the PRD prompt (use “Copy the PRD prompt”; it is also at the end of the PDF) and answer Claude’s questions one at a time.

    Project Explorer · AI Builder Space

    Fall 2026, 15.S23 AI Builder Space (MIT Sloan): 65 projects in Sprint 1 and 79 in Sprint 2 (72 new and 7 improvements of Sprint 1 projects). 137 distinct projects. Search by name or combine the filters, then click a project to see its full details.

    Filters

    Stage is estimated from what each PRD or Product Brief says, so it may be behind the real status. Sources: Sprint 1 PRDs, the Sprint 2 Product Briefs (Nov 2–9, 2026) and the PRD 2 Dashboard. Summaries were written from the documents. For Sprint 2 projects, the classification (project type, form factor, role of AI and level) is a provisional reading of the brief and uses the same rules as Sprint 1. Projects that continue from Sprint 1 are shown once, tagged Sprint 1 + Sprint 2, with a "What's new in Sprint 2" block. The level measures technical difficulty for a beginner, not the quality of the idea. Contains student names and project content: share with course staff only.
